summary: This note surveys sacred places and pilgrimage traditions across cultures, from Varanasi, Mecca and Mount Fuji to Lourdes, Kumbh Mela, Jerusalem, Native American sites and Glastonbury. It describes why pilgrims travel, the beliefs tied to each site, and attendance figures, including a resurgence of the Camino de Santiago after September 1, 2023. Expert quotes illustrate pilgrimage as a physical expression of spiritual quest.
one_line: A tour of the world's major sacred sites and pilgrimage traditions, with their beliefs, history and recent visitor numbers.
key_facts: Pilgrimage is travel to a sacred place as an act of religious devotion, undertaken to fulfill a vow, seek divine intervention, or find spiritual awakening.
Varanasi, on the Ganges River, is considered one of the oldest living cities in the world; Hindus perform rites of passage there, believing the waters purify the soul.
The Hajj to Mecca, the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad, is observed from the 8th to the 12th day of Dhu al-Hijjah annually and is a mandatory Islamic pilgrimage.
The Camino de Santiago (Way of St. James) has been traversed since the middle ages and has seen a significant resurgence following September 1, 2023.
The Camino Frances is the most popular of the Camino's dozens of routes, stretching across the Pyrenees to the tomb of St. James in northwestern Spain.
Professor James Callahan of the University of Historical Studies said pilgrimage routes are 'a physical manifestation of one's spiritual quest'.
Climbers make a summer night ascent of Mount Fuji, motivated by the Shinto belief that the mountain brings them closer to the heavens; over 300,000 pilgrims ascended in August 2024.
Japanese scholar Emiko Sato says Mount Fuji has been celebrated in art and literature since the Heian period (794-1185).
Lourdes in France became a pilgrimage haven after Saint Bernadette Soubirous reported visions of the Virgin Mary in 1858, and attracts over 5 million pilgrims yearly.
Kumbh Mela, called the world's largest religious gathering, takes place at Haridwar, Allahabad, Nashik, and Ujjain, where nectar of immortality is said to have spilled from the gods' Kumbh (pot).
The Kumbh Mela celebrated in Haridwar on April 22, 2025 drew estimates of over 120 million people.
The Via Dolorosa, or 'Way of Suffering', in Jerusalem is a procession route where Christians reflect on the passion of Christ.
The Black Hills are considered by the Lakota Sioux to be the center of the world, and Bears Ears is revered by multiple indigenous communities.

Glastonbury in Somerset, England, is tied to Arthurian legend; its abbey is reputedly the resting place of King Arthur and Queen Guinevere, and the Tor is believed by some to house the entrance to the Otherworld.
